March 22, 2025
IFW Committee members,
My name is Adele Morgan. I live in Richmond. I'm writing in support of LD 976.
In May 2022 the U. S. Coast Guard ordered the cessation of the only public transportation to Swan Island. Since the ferry stopped:
 Local supervised school groups have stopped their regular visits, depriving young people of their local history and wildlife education.
 Environmental Studies Classes from Bowdoin College no longer visit every semester. Those students will lack exposure to the unique story Swan Island has to tell.
 Local businesses, like Annabella's, The Old Goat and Kimberly's have lost seasonal customer's.

Regular transportation will return schoolchildren to the island, be an economic driver for Richmond businesses and give the historic buildings on the island a chance to survive. Local fundraising for historic preservation will occur only if there is an awareness of need.

Adele Morgan

Testimony of Rep. Allison Hepler in support of
LD 976, Resolve, to Restore Accessible Public Transportation to
Swan Island in Perkins Township
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
Good afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts, and members of the Inland Fisheries
and Wildlife Committee. I am Allison I-Iepler and I represent the towns of Arrowsic,
Georgetown, Phippsburg, West Bath and Woolwich. I am here today in support of LD 976,
Resolve, to Restore Accessible Public Transportation to Swan Island in Perkins Township.
As you have heard ~ or will hear -- today, Swan Island is a very special place in a very special
part of the Kennebec River at the head of Merrymeeting Bay. It is currently managed by IFW as the Steve Powell Wildlife Management Area and, in the words of IFW's Management Plan,
"This unique area serves as a wildlife management area, wildlife refuge, and a public educational and recreational facility."
There are many good reasons to help IFW restore accessible public transportation to this island, but I'm a historian so I'm going to speak a little bit about the significance of its history, and the
historical remnants that still remain on the island.
Pre-colonial indigenous people who lived on the island camped there in the summer and harvested the wild rice that can still be seen on the southern end of the island. The first Europeans to see Swan Island were likely French explorers sailing with Samuel De Champlain when he visited the Kennebec in 1605. The island also hosted shipbuilding and ice harvesting
industries.
The visible history that remains -- the history you will see when you visit -- comes from two early settlers, one a Loyalist, Silvester Gardiner whose daughter and husband lived in what is today known as the Gardiner-Dumaresq House. It was built in the war-tom years of the late 1750s and
is the oldest surviving house on the island, it's remarkable that it still stands.
Another prominent home that still stands was built by Samuel Tubbs, one of General Washington's commanding officers. It became known as the Tubbs-Reed house in the 1830s. These buildings capture the imagination of visitors wondering what it was like to live here 200
years ago.

District 49: Arrowsic, Georgetown, Phippsburg, West Bath and Woolwich

Finally, for those of us who are excited about the nation's 250"` birthday, or semiquincentennial, Swan Island holds an additional attraction, the ghosts of Col. Benedict Arnold and his crew from Boston stopping at the island on their way to Pittston, just upriver, to pick up 220 battoes, with
which they would attempt an attack of Quebec.
We hope that real, live "ghosts" from the Arnold Expedition Historical Society will land on
Swan Island this summer by battoe.
My point is that Swan Island is a state treasure, not only for its natural resources, but for its
historical ones as well. Swan Island offers a landscape of the past. And I hope we can find a way
to safely welcome the public. Thank you.
District 49: Arrowsic, Georgetown, Phippsburg, West Bath and Woolwich

10038316:
For : LD 976 "Resolve, to Restore Accessible Public Transportation to Swan Island in Perkins Township"
My name is Amanda McDaniel, and I am the secretary of the Friends of Swan Island, and a resident of Richmond, Maine.
In 2024, IF&W put out a beautiful video marketing Swan Island as "Unique Access to a Unique Place". Please rename it "Potentially Deadly Access to a Unique Place."
Unless you are rich enough to own a boat, lucky enough to have a friend with one, or physically strong enough to navigate the extremely powerful tidal current of the Kennebec River, you cannot gain access.
If you have a boat, you have to be additionally lucky that there are no other boats docked at the campground side, it's too small.
We had three women in their sixties come from hours away, so excited to get on Swan Island. They weren't strong enough to kayak, so we said we would help them out. We found a date, checked the weather and tides. We tried to dock at the campground but two small boats were already there. We floated around for hours, waiting to see if they might leave. These women had to go back to their homes having never stepped foot on the island. Are we proud of this?
Is Unique Access really just two small boats per day in the high season?
Elderly people are out. People with disabilities are out. Children's groups are out.
Worse than all of this loss, someone could die just trying to get out to the island. We have witnessed canoes almost capsizing in strong wake. In several cases, we've seen canoeists being rescued and towed back to the mainland. The everyday person is not equipped to understand the Kennebec River, ... especially not tourists. So now tourists are out.
If you were to jump off the dock at the Richmond Waterfront Park and swim out a little further than 6 feet when the tide is going out, it can pull you out before you know it. The surface can be glassy and calm, meanwhile, entire toppled trees are rushing past just below the surface.
In between Swan and Little Swan, where the campground dock sits.. it's even worse. I've had many experiences trying to hold our boat to the dock and had to let go of the rope. Shoulder, wrist and back injuries are coming for all visitors to the campground dock.

If you are in a kayak going from the Richmond waterfront up and around the north end of the island to the campground, you are inevitably going against the tide on one side or the other. The double pull of an outgoing tide with the rushing river can't be underestimated.
The ferry provided the safest route for visitors to the island.
I would not want to be the State of Maine when a child dies because their family wanted to go camping, loaded up their canoe and a motor boat passes, with wake filling the boat.
Let's spend the money, find the resources, and make this a safe passage to one of the most important, historic, peaceful and beautiful islands on the eastern seaboard.
I'm happy to answer any questions you may have.
10038407:
My name is Gary Smith and I am a charter boat captain with River Run Tours operating out of Bath. I have circumnavigated Swan Island on numerous occasions for our passengers. Swan Island is not only beautiful to observe from the water but is even more special when one can experience its beauty, history, wildlife, and recreational opportunities on the island.
The general public was able to access Swan Island safely when the ferry was operating however today, access to the island is limited to those with boats, kayaks, and canoes. I have personally boated and kayaked to Swan Island and with years of experience with both, access to the only dock available to boaters and when non-boaters are paddling against the current can be challenging if not dangerous for those not familiar with tidal waters. At particular times during the tides, the currents can be rapid resulting in fatigue to kayakers and difficulty docking for boaters on the camp side, floating dock.
Since the termination of the ferry service to Swan Island, both residents and visitors of Maine have lost the opportunity to experience a gem that offers so much. Its rich history, wildlife viewing, recreational opportunities, and conservation efforts are experience based opportunities for youths and adults. To inspire future Maine historians and conservationists should be a primary mission of Swan Island. These opportunities should be available to all and not limited to a few. The town of Richmond would also benefit economically if ferry service was restored. Visitors are likely to patronize the businesses in Richmond when planning a trip to Swan Island.
To quote the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife's website page, "Swan Island, at the head of Merrymeeting Bay, welcomes hikers, campers, birders, anglers, wildlife watchers and explorers to its shores for an unforgettable Maine experience." It is time to restore the ferry service to Swan Island so that all can have the opportunity for an unforgettable Maine experience.
Captain Gary Smith

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife March 24, 2025
Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and esteemed members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee, I am Senator Denise Tepler and I represent District #24 -- all of Sagadahoc County, the town of Dresden in Lincoln County, and Perkins Township. My testimony is in support of L.D. 976, Resolve, to Restore Accessible Public Transportation to Swan Island in Perkins Township.
I am writing to let you know how important the return of this ferry service is to my constituents. Currently, Swan Island is only accessible to those who are well off enough to own a power boat or hale and hearty enough to row or paddle to the island. Many of my constituents in this area are elderly and poor. Yet, they love Swan Island.
It used to be a place where the community would gather for lobster bakes annually. It used to be a place where school children went to learn about the environment on an island that has wild places and formerly cultivated places.
Without the ferry service, these things cannot happen. Boy Scout and Girl Scout troops can no longer plan group camping trips to Swan Island. People can't take the ferry simply for a stroll in a safe, quiet and wild place nearby.
One of my elder constituents was nearly in tears while I sat at her kitchen table in Richmond, describing how much she missed going out to Swan Island.
Bringing the ferry back will bring back equity in the use of this state land, it will bring back a community ownership feeling to the island, it will bring back educational opportunities for area children. Please bring back regular ferry service to Swan Island in Perkins Township.

Dear Friends, My name is Gary Carter and I am teacher at the Richmond Middle School. Swan Island (known years ago as "Swango Island" due to the habitat it provided for American Bald Eagles) has forever had an attachment and connection to the community of Richmond. Once housing a full time Game Warden and providing access and enjoyment for all of Maine's residents, this beautiful "gem" has suffered from years of neglect which discouraged those of us who love its beauty. During the nineties, the Richmond School Department partnered with many to initiate exploration, restoration and nature/history studies of multiple kinds. Buildings were researched, biographies written, former residents studied, habitat and ecosystems explored. A whole generation of Richmond students, as well as many from other schools, were transported regularly to explore and enjoy. Over the past decade visitation and use of the island has dwindled for many reasons. Whatever the sum of those reasons, the time to restore access to this island is long overdue for all. The Richmond School Department (Specifically our Middle School) was recognized for its efforts and the programs we established for learning during our affiliation with the "Swan Island Project." I am supremely confident that we would welcome the opportunity to begin to return to the island and rekindle the vast learning activities it provides. I believe other schools would follow and a whole new generation of young people would have the benefit of exploring this beautiful "natural classroom." This is just one facet of what restoring access to the island would provide. The whole state and our friends who visit from other locales, would be able to explore and enjoy all the island has to offer. Its history is rich. Providing housing for many who worked in the ice industry. Hosting visitation by many who traveled the "underground railroad" on their way to the Arnold Trail and continuing on to Canada to secure their freedom. Providing material and cover for Fort Richmond, which sat on the intersection of the river north and south. It is a part of our American history...in so many ways. It is time for Swan Island to be part of our American future...connecting generations with what was and what can be. TESTIMONY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
IN OPPOSITION TO L.D. 976
"RESOLVE, TO RESTORE ACCESSIBLE PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION TO SWAN ISLAND IN PERKINS TOWNSHIP"
Presented by Representative CLUCHEY of Bowdoinham.
Cosponsored by Senator TEPLER of Sagadahoc and Representatives: BRIDGEO of Augusta, HEPLER of Woolwich, LEMELIN of Chelsea.
DATE OF HEARING: March 24, 2025
Good afternoon Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee. I am Nate Webb, Wildlife Division Director at the
Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, speaking on behalf of the Department in opposition to L.D. 976.
This resolve directs the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife to develop a plan to
ensure that accessible, regularly scheduled public transportation is available to Swan Island in Perkins Township in Sagadahoc County.
The Steve Powell Wildlife Management Area, owned and managed by the Maine
Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW), is located on the Kennebec River
between the towns of Richmond and Dresden. It is an unorganized township and subject to the jurisdiction of the Maine Land Use Planning Commission. It includes Swan Island, Little Swan Island, and several hundred acres of tidal flats totaling about 1,755 acres. In 1995, the United States Department of Interior placed the island on the National Register of Historic Places in recognition of the historic architectural homesteads and landscape of
the island.
The Department acquired the WMA using United States Fish and Wildlife Service
(USFWS) Federal Aid in Wildlife Restoration funding starting in the l940's to meet the
mission and purpose of the WMA system, which is to provide a statewide, ecologically
based system of land holdings for the protection and enhancement of important wildlife habitats that also provide opportunities for public recreation, where those forms of
recreation do not unduly impact wildlife resources. More specifically, Swan Island was
acquired for the specific purpose of protecting important waterfowl habitat at the head of Merrymeeting Bay.

In the mid-1960's, the Department established a campground on the WMA and began
offering transportation to the island. For decades, we continued offering the ferry service
to the WMA, even as we lost permanent staff capacity and began relying on seasonal
contractors. To help offset the cost of providing transportation and the seasonal positions,
we implemented a day-use and overnight camping fee structure.
Several recent events have led to a change in our approach towards public access to the
WMA including:
l. A determination by the United States Coast Guard that the vessel was being
operated as a small passenger vessel and therefore needed proper inspections and certifications and associated licensure of the captain and deckhands appropriate to the horsepower and tonnage of the vessel.
2. The loss of seasonal housing on the WMA due to mold, lead paint and other
unsafe conditions associated with the staff house.
3. A changed emphasis by the Department on public outreach and communications
to venues and formats that maximize public engagement.
For these reasons, the Department has worked to realign its operations with financial and staff capacity and to ensure that the island is being managed consistent with the purpose
of our WMA system. Recent rulemaking removed any access fees associated with the
WMA, making it consistent with the 71 other state~owned WMAs. We also transitioned to a self-access approach for the WMA, again, consistent with all other WMAs.
Re-establishing a regular ferry service to the WMA would require significant staff and
financial resources, such that other necessary work and priorities within the Department would be impacted. The Department believes that self-access, or access provided by other entities, is the most effective way to provide access to the island, and in fact,
several entities now offer transportation to the island. This allows the Department to
focus its limited capacity on facility maintenance and habitat management.
The Department recognizes the historic and cultural importance of Swan Island and we
are interested in cooperating with groups to maintain the historic structures and deliver educational programming focused on historical and cultural topics in balance with the purpose of conservation.
I would be glad to answer any questions at this time or during the work session.

LD 976: Resolve, to Restore Accessible Public Transportation to Swan Island in Perkins Township
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife

Good afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts, and members of the Inland Fisheries and

Wildlife Committee. My name is Sally Cluchey, and I represent House District 52, which includes the
communities of Bowdoin, Bowdoinham, Richmond, and Perkins Island Township. I Qam here today to
present LD 976: Resolve, to Restore Accessible Public Transportation to Swan Islantl in Perkins

Township.

i

Swan Island is a 2,000-acre wildlife management area located in the Kennebec River between Richmond and Dresden. It is owned and managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (IFW) as part of the Steve Powell Wildlife Management Area. This unique resource combines conservation, outdoor recreation, historical preservation, and education, offering opriortunities that few other places in Maine provide. -

For decades, Swan Island has provided public access for wildlife conservation education, learn-to-hunt programs, camping, and historical preservation efforts. It became a hub for outdoor learning, attracting school groups, researchers, and visitors. The island provides important habitat for bald eagles,
white-tailed deer, and migratory birds, offering hands-on learning experiences in conservation
management. Swan Island is also home to remnants of the town of Perkins, one of Maine's earliest settlements, with five standing homes dating from the late 18th and early 19th centuries, a cemetery with
headstones dating from 1802-1968, and the entire island listed in the National Register of Historic
Places. Families, scouts, and outdoor enthusiasts have utilized Swan Island for overnight camping, hiking, biking, and exploring Maine's natural and cultural heritage.

Historically, ferry service provided access to the island, allowing visitors to enjoy these resources.
However, in 2022, ferry service was discontinued, drastically reducing public accessf and limiting the ability of the community and the state to fully benefit from this resource.

District 52: Bowdoinham, Richmond and Bowdoin (part)
;
i

The ferry was discontinued primarily due to aging infrastructure and evolving U.S. Coast Guard regulations that require compliance with updated vessel inspection and staffing requirements. Without a compliant vessel and with the pier in need of repairs, safe and reliable feny service became infeasible.
As a result, access toi the island is now severely restricted, with only those who can launch their own
'
boats able to visit.
The loss of ferry service has negatively affected Richmond's economy, particularly tourism-related businesses. Swan Island was once a popular destination for families and outdoor enthusiasts, generating revenue for local businesses. Visitors would start the day with breakfast at Annabella's, take the ferry for an afternoon of hiking, wildlife viewing, and exploring the beaver pond, then return to town for pizza at The Old Goat and ice cream at Maine Street Dairy Treat. Without reliable ferry access, these kinds of experiences--and the economic benefits they brought to Richmond--have disappeared. Restoring ferry service is not just about recreation; it's about revitalizing the local economy.
The closure has also created a significant loss in educational opportunities. Richmond schools, in particular, actively participated in educational programs related to Swan Island, providing valuable experiential learning opportunities for students. One such program, The Life and Death of a Small Maine Town, delved into the history of Perkins. With its historic homes, cemetery, and the island's rich legacy of shipbuilding, farming, and ice harvesting, Swan Island was an invaluable resource for teaching Social Studies and Maine's history. Without ferry access, students can no longer experience this hands-on
S
learning in a way that fosters a deeper connection to local ecology and history.
Restoring ferry access to Swan Island is critical not only for local tourism and education, but also for maintaining compliance with public access requirements for lands funded by the Pittman-Robertson Act. Lands purchased or managed with Pittman-Robertson funds, such as Swan Island, are required to be
open to the public for wildlife-related recreation, including activities like hiking, wildlife observation, and educational programs. Since hunting is not allowed on the island, it becomes even more important to provide access to other activities that allow the public to engage with the island's wildlife and natural resources. Developing a plan to restore ferry access is the first step in ensuring the public can continue
to experience Swan Island and fully benefit from this public resource.
The process of restoring ferry access involves two key steps: rebuilding the pier and developing a
transportation plan. This Committee voted unanimously to recommend that the AFA Committee
W appropriate $150,000 in general funds to match $350,000 in federal funds for pier repairs. LD 976
directs IF to develop a transportation plan for restoring reliable ferry service. This will allow the department to evaluate flexible, cost-effective options for ferry service, such as part-time operations during weekends or peak visitation seasons.
Reinstating ferry service comes with challenges, particularly with compliance to U.S. Coast Guard
regulations, which require significant operational costs. However, there may be a way forward through
discussions with the Coast Guard to seek a limited exemption that allows for a more cost-effective, part-time ferry service. Perhaps this could be a public-private partnership. Finding a sustainable solution does not necessarily mean restoring past service exactly as it was, but rather developing a feasible access model that balances cost and community benefit.
District 52: Bowdoinham, Richmond and Bowdoin (part)

That is the good faith effort that this bill seeks. Swan Island is a publicly owned resource that should be
accessible to the people of Maine. The first step--rebuilding the pier---~is already in motion. LD 976 will allow us to take the next step by directing IFW to create a viable transportation plan to restore feny access in a sustainable and responsible way. I urge the committee to support LD 976-and to help restore
public access to one of Maine's treasured public lands. Thank you for your time and consideration. I welcome any questions.

To whom it may concern,
I am writing as the manager of Annabella's Restaurant in Richmond, Maine, in support of the reinstatement of the ferry service from Richmond to Swan Island. As a business person here in Richmond, I have witnessed firsthand the positive impact that ferry access to Swan Island could have, not just for our restaurant, but for the entire community.
During the summer months, Richmond sees a significant increase in visitors, and many of these tourists are drawn by the beauty and unique charm of Swan Island. The ferry service would provide a vital link between the mainland and this incredible natural resource, encouraging more visitors to explore the island while benefiting the local economy. At Annabella's, we have noticed an uptick in foot traffic and, therefore, business during the summer months when Swan Island is easily accessible. Reinstalling the ferry service would undoubtedly continue to drive this growth, making Richmond an even more attractive destination for tourists.
However, the value of this ferry service extends far beyond economic benefits. For our community, Swan Island holds cultural and historical significance, and many residents have long relied on the island for recreational and educational purposes. Whether it's for a day of hiking, fishing, or simply enjoying the outdoors, Swan Island offers an unparalleled experience for locals, and easy access to it would enhance the quality of life for those who call Richmond home.
Additionally, ferry access to Swan Island would help build a stronger sense of place in Richmond. When people can easily visit a nearby natural treasure, it fosters a deeper connection to the land, history, and community. The ferry service would serve as a symbolic bridge, not just between Richmond and Swan Island, but between our town's past, present, and future. It would reinforce our identity as a welcoming and vibrant community where people can come together to enjoy the beauty that surrounds us.
Finally, the tourism draw provided by ferry service to Swan Island is undeniable. Richmond, with its rich history and stunning waterfront, is a town that thrives on tourism. Visitors who come to explore Swan Island often find themselves returning to experience more of what our town has to offer. The ferry service would bring additional foot traffic to local businesses, helping to sustain our economy, create jobs, and support the small businesses that are the lifeblood of our community.
In conclusion, the reinstatement of the ferry service from Richmond to Swan Island is not only a step toward enriching our local economy but also an opportunity to strengthen our community's connection to this beautiful, historically significant island.
